props.title: Airport
props.initialSlug: Disaster looms as bomb threatens snowbound plane

sections.content: Airport launched the disaster film boom of the 1970s, setting the template that countless films would follow. Based on Arthur Hailey's bestseller, it features an all-star cast including Burt Lancaster, Dean Martin, and Helen Hayes, who won an Oscar for her role as a stowaway. The film's multiple intersecting plotlines - a bomber on board, a snowstorm, relationship drama - established the disaster genre's signature format of interweaving personal stories with spectacular peril. Its massive success ($100+ million on a $10 million budget) directly inspired The Poseidon Adventure (1972) and The Towering Inferno (1974), creating Hollywood's disaster obsession.

sections.content: The success of Airport spawned three direct sequels - Airport 1975 (1975), Airport '77 (1977), and The Concorde... Airport '79 (1979) - each trying to top the previous film's spectacle. The franchise's increasing absurdity eventually led to its brilliant parody in Airplane! (1980), which copied scenes directly from Zero Hour! (1957) while mocking disaster film clichés. The Airport series' influence extends beyond parody though - modern disaster films like The Day After Tomorrow (2004) and 2012 (2009) still use its formula of personal drama amid catastrophe.

Airport's technical achievements were groundbreaking for 1970. The film used innovative special effects to create its harrowing airplane sequences, earning Oscar nominations for cinematography, art direction, costume design, and sound. Its success also influenced aviation thrillers like Skyjacked (1972) and Airport '77 (1977), which copied its mix of technical accuracy and human drama. Even contemporary films like Sully (2016) and Flight (2012) owe a debt to Airport's realistic portrayal of aviation crisis management. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Modern Impact

sections.content: While often dismissed as melodramatic, Airport's influence on blockbuster filmmaking can't be overstated. Its blend of spectacle and human drama created the template for event movies, directly influencing films like The Day After Tomorrow (2004) and San Andreas (2015). The film's multiple-storyline approach also impacted non-disaster films, with directors like Robert Altman citing it as inspiration for his overlapping narrative style in films like Nashville (1975).
